analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to dismiss Chapter 11 filings corporations use to escape mass-tort debts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one Democrat and one Republican backing it, died in the House Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Some large companies facing huge lawsuit bills split themselves in two, move the lawsuits onto a hollowed-out shell, and have the shell file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The lawsuits get frozen and eventually settled against a company with little money, while the profitable parent company walks away shielded from paying victims in full. This bill would let bankruptcy judges throw out those filings as bad-faith or futile, end the freeze that protects the parent company from being sued, and make it easier to hold parent companies, officers, and insurers financially responsible for injuries like asbestos or toxic-product exposure.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who are creditors of large companies — especially victims of mass injuries like asbestos, toxic products, or opioids, and their families. Under current law their claims often get funneled into a deliberately weakened shell company's bankruptcy, and the solvent parent gets a release. The bill would let courts dismiss those setups as bad faith, keep the lawsuits alive against the parent company, and speed up bankruptcies that currently drag on to wear creditors down.

how_it_helps.text: Lets bankruptcy judges dismiss a Chapter 11 case that is 'objectively futile' or filed in 'subjective bad faith,' and puts the burden of proof on the company doing the filing.

Presumes bad faith when a company manufactured the venue for its bankruptcy, and makes that presumption hard to rebut — aimed at forum-shopping where companies file in whichever court rules are friendliest.

Creates a conclusive presumption of bad faith for companies that used a divisional merger or restructuring in the prior four years, or that filed to cap their liability to creditors they actually have the money to pay in full.

Ends the automatic stay (the freeze on lawsuits once bankruptcy is filed) for claims against parent companies, officers, insurers, and financiers connected to a debtor that restructured within four years — so mass-injury claimants can pursue the entities with real assets.
Defines the protected claims broadly enough to cover exposure to a product, material, or substance affecting at least 100 people, such as asbestos or toxic-chemical victims.
Caps how long a company can take to reorganize in Chapter 11 at 24 months instead of an open-ended 'reasonable period.'

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations facing mass-tort liability, their shareholders and executives, private equity owners, and their insurers, who would lose the ability to use a restructured bankruptcy to cap what they owe injured people. Some troubled companies that restructure legitimately could also face more litigation against their parents.

drawbacks.text: Critics of limits on this tactic argue that non-debtor releases and stays are sometimes the only way to settle mass torts fairly, since without them creditors can sue a solvent parent instead of accepting an orderly settlement fund — potentially leaving some victims with nothing after prolonged litigation. The bill does not ban releases outright, but restricting the stay and dismissal tools pushes in that direction.

The bill's conclusive presumptions are harsh: a company that did any divisional merger or restructuring within four years would automatically be presumed to be filing in bad faith, with the burden on the debtor — a rule that could sweep in legitimate reorganizations and make it harder or costlier for struggling companies to restructure and preserve jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific, widely criticized maneuver — the 'Texas two-step' — where companies manufacture a bankruptcy to shrink what they owe injured people while protecting profitable parents. The benefit to mass-tort victims is real and targeted. The cost is that its strong presumptions could also complicate legitimate restructurings of genuinely distressed companies, which can put jobs at risk; the bill does not appear to carve out fine distinctions between abusive and reorganizational filings beyond a general 'valid reorganizational purpose' test.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes introduced the bill on July 23, 2024, joined by Reps. Jerrold Nadler and Tony Gooden of Texas, giving it sponsorship from both parties.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the bill's action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies that restructure to cap their liability to mass-tort creditors are better off, since the limits never took effect; injured claimants remain in the position the bill was written to fix.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.role: U.S. Representative (NY-12), senior Judiciary Committee member

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat without action from July 2024 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from birth: a Democratic sponsor and senior Democratic Judiciary member joined by one Republican cosponsor, and it never reached the stage where party-line voting could occur.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and corporations facing mass-tort liability
industries.note: The bill's target: companies that split into a liability shell and a protected parent, then file Chapter 11 to cap what they pay asbestos, toxic-product, or other mass-tort victims. The bill would let courts dismiss those filings and keep claims alive against the asset-rich parent.

industries.industry: Private equity and corporate restructuring players
industries.note: Divisional mergers and restructurings within four years of a bankruptcy filing trigger a presumption of bad faith under the bill, raising the cost and risk of the leveraged-split strategies some sponsors and lenders rely on.

industries.industry: Insurers and lenders to restructured companies
industries.note: The bill ends bankruptcy-stay protection for claims against insurers, financiers, and advice-providers connected to a restructured debtor, exposing them to direct lawsuits from mass-injury claimants.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy and restructuring professionals (law firms, advisors)
industries.note: Fewer lucrative two-step bankruptcies to run, but more contested dismissals and non-debtor litigation to advise on; the effect on the profession cuts both ways.
